questions.knowledge_point: Determining Components of Orthogonal Vectors in Inner Product Spaces of Polynomials
questions.problem:
Let $V={R}_{1}[t]$ be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most $1,$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=x(1)y(1)+x(3)y(3).
$$

If $p(t)=t-1$ and $q(t)=kt+3$ are orthogonal with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V,$ then $k=$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $p(t)$ and $q(t)$ are orthogonal, their inner product must be zero.

First, we compute the inner product using our definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨p(t),q(t)⟩ & =p(1)q(1)+p(3)q(3) \\  & =(1-1)(k+3)+(3-1)(3k+3) \\  & =0+(6k+6) \\  & =6k+6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set $⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=0$ and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨p(t),q(t)⟩ & =0 \\ 6k+6 & =0 \\ 6k & =-6 \\ k & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V={R}_{1}[t]$ be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most $1,$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=x(-1)y(-1)+x(1)y(1).
$$

If $p(t)=3t+1$ and $q(t)=2t+k$ are orthogonal with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V,$ then $k=$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $p(t)$ and $q(t)$ are orthogonal, their inner product must be zero.

First, we compute the inner product using our definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨p(t),q(t)⟩ & =p(-1)q(-1)+p(1)q(1) \\  & =(-3+1)(-2+k)+(3+1)(2+k) \\  & =(4-2k)+(8+4k) \\  & =12+2k \\  & =2k+12\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set $⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=0$ and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨p(t),q(t)⟩ & =0 \\ 2k+12 & =0 \\ 2k & =-12 \\ k & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Components of Orthogonal Vectors in Inner Product Spaces of Continuous Functions
questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,2]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,2],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

If $x(t)={t}^{2}-2t$ and $y(t)=k-t$ are orthogonal with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V,$ then $k=$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ are orthogonal, their inner product must be zero.

First, we compute the inner product using our definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x(t),y(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({t}^{2}-2t)(k-t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}((2+k){t}^{2}-2kt-{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{(2+k){t}^{3}}{3}-k{t}^{2}-\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}){|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8(2+k)}{3}-4k-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set $⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=0$ and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x(t),y(t)⟩ & =0 \\ \frac{8(2+k)}{3}-4k-4 & =0 \\ \frac{8(2+k)}{3} & =4k+4 \\ 8(2+k) & =12k+12 \\ 2(2+k) & =3k+3 \\ 4+2k & =3k+3 \\ k & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About Orthogonal Vectors in Inner Product Spaces
questions.problem:
Let $V=C[-1,0]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[-1,0],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{0}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Given the functions $f(t)=t$ and $g(t)=\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}},$ which of the following statements are true?

- $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=-\frac{1}{3}$
- $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=0$
- $f(t)⊥g(t)$ with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to evaluate 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{0}t\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=1-{t}^{2},$ $\text{d}u=-2t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}t\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & =-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3/2}]-[-\frac{1}{3}(0)^{3/2}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now examine the statements:

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. This is as a result of the above calculations.

- Statement III is false. Since the inner product is not zero, our vectors are not orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[0,\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Given the functions $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ and $g(t)=1,$ which of the following statements are true?

- $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=\pi $
- $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=0$
- $f(t)⊥g(t)$ with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to evaluate

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can evaluate this integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t & ={[-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}{2}|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi )}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now examine the statements:

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. This is as a result of the above calculations.

- Statement III is true. Since the inner product is zero, our vectors must be orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."
